tldr: We propose a system where a single low-cost camera worn on the collector's head tracks the pose and jaw width of an electronics-free glove while simultaneously providing visual observations for the policy, and at deployment, a compact arm mimics the head's motion to achieve high-precision robot execution.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed system. (a) The collector wears a head camera and manipulates an electronics-free 3D-printed glove in the workspace. (b) The head-camera view: 6-DoF gripper pose and jaw width are computed simultaneously from the marker sphere (red), jaw markers (blue/yellow), and paper tiles on the desk (green). (c) At deployment, the same camera is mounted on a low-cost 6-axis arm beside the robot, mimicking human head movement based on end-effector motion.
overview:
In robot imitation learning, collecting demonstration data using handheld devices decoupled from the robot (such as UMI) is gaining significant attention. However, conventional methods place heavy equipment on the wrist—including cameras, SLAM sensors, IMUs, or VR controllers—along with cumbersome cables. This creates considerable overhead for synchronizing and cross-calibrating multiple sensor streams. Furthermore, wrist cameras only capture the immediate surroundings of the hand, introducing field-of-view issues such as losing sight of the goal receptacle during transport.

To address this, the authors observed that "human gaze naturally precedes hand motion." They devised a simple setup where a single camera ($122) worn on the collector's head handles both policy visual observations and hand tracking. The glove ($22) is a purely mechanical replica without any electronics, bearing only printed fiducials. During deployment, the same camera is mounted on a low-cost, compact servo arm ($122) placed next to the robot, which mimics the collector's head movements based on the robot's joint state, closing the viewpoint gap between data collection and execution.

In experiments, the hand pose labels estimated from the head camera achieved high accuracy, with a median error of 6.5 mm and 1.6° against robot encoders. In real-robot trials, adding 194 glove demonstrations to just 48 teleoperated episodes via co-training significantly boosted success from 10/25 to 17/25, matching the performance of 172 purely teleoperated episodes (18/25). In viewpoint comparisons, the head camera achieved a success rate of 20/25, outperforming both the wrist camera (15/25) and a fixed camera (12/25), demonstrating the decisive advantage of combining a wide field of view with tracking capability.
contributions: Building a lightweight demonstration system that self-labels 6-DoF poses and jaw width using only an electronics-free $22 3D-printed glove and a single $122 head camera
Proposing a dynamic camera system that faithfully reproduces human head motion from robot joint states using a low-cost compact arm, bridging the viewpoint gap at deployment
Demonstrating that the head-mounted perspective avoids the critical blind spot of wrist cameras—losing sight of the goal during transport—and significantly improves real-robot manipulation success
Showing that co-training glove demonstrations with a small amount of teleoperated data achieves performance comparable to collecting roughly three times as much teleoperated data

sections.heading: Why put the camera on the collector's "head" instead of the wrist?
sections.summary: By consolidating the heavy wrist-mounted payload and synchronization hassles of conventional UMI into a single head camera, the system captures the entire workspace without hand occlusions, leveraging the human habit of leading hand motions with gaze.
sections.details:
Robot data collection via teleoperation completely ties up both the real robot and the operator's time. In contrast, handheld devices offer the major advantage of collecting data in parallel without requiring the physical robot.

However, conventional UMI (Universal Manipulation Interface) setups have major drawbacks. Mounting cameras, SLAM sensors, IMUs, or VR controllers on the wrist makes the hand heavy, requiring users to manage cables, timestamp synchronization across multiple sensors, and cross-calibration. In addition, wrist cameras have their field of view locked to the gripper direction; the moment the gripper lifts an object and turns, target containers can easily fall outside the frame.

To overcome this, the authors proposed consolidating everything into a single camera worn on the head. When humans perform tasks, their gaze naturally shifts ahead of hand movements. By adopting a head-mounted viewpoint, the hand is not occluded by the collector's body, and both the hand and the workspace remain inside the frame at a comfortable distance. The glove carries zero electronics: by simply reading printed fiducials with the head camera, the system simultaneously extracts the 6-DoF gripper pose and jaw width. At deployment, a compact arm beside the robot mimics the collector's head motion, naturally resolving the viewpoint shift.

sections.heading: Hardware under $260 and the viewpoint-mimicking mechanism
sections.summary: The system consists of an electronics-free glove, a head camera, paper marker tiles, and a compact tracking arm to reproduce viewpoints. An automated pipeline extracts accurate end-effector poses and jaw widths solely from head camera footage.
sections.details:
### Collection Hardware
The demonstration glove is 3D-printed to replicate the exact geometry of the robot's gripper (YAM gripper), without any actuators or electronics. On the back of the hand sits a 15 mm regular dodecahedron (marker sphere) covered with 11 ArUco markers, while each jaw is fitted with a wedge-shaped tail bearing 5 AprilTags to measure jaw width. The glove's parts cost only $22. The collector mounts a 4K camera ($122) onto a GoPro head strap and records at 15 Hz. Setup requires only taping four AprilTag tiles (60 mm) to the tabletop as spatial references. This enables rapid recording of pick-and-place actions at 2.0 to 3.1 episodes per minute, outpacing teleoperation (1.6 episodes per minute).

### Self-Labeling from the Head Camera
From each frame, the pipeline simultaneously extracts three quantities: (1) camera pose relative to the tabletop tiles, (2) hand pose via PnP calculations on the marker sphere, and (3) jaw width from the inter-marker distance on the jaws. Combining these yields the gripper pose in workspace coordinates. To prevent tracking dropouts caused by head turns, the layout of the tiles is automatically re-estimated from multi-tile views, allowing smooth pose continuity under velocity clamping even when only a single tile is visible. Frame dropout ranges from only 0.7% to 7.4%, far lower than the occlusion dropout observed with a fixed external camera (8% to 22%).

### Building the Robot's "Head" with a Compact Arm
During robot execution, an open-source 6-axis arm (SO-101, parts cost $122) is installed beside the robot, carrying the same camera at its tip. This arm receives only the robot's end-effector joint encoders as input and mimics the collector's head turns recorded during data collection. Specifically, it combines a fixed-gain controller that keeps looking toward the hand with a ridge regression model that predicts the relative displacement of the head to the hand. This reproduces nearly identical framing (normalized centroids of 0.37/0.62 vs. 0.38/0.60) with a 0.4 s tracking lag.

### Dataset and Training
Policy learning employs ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers), where glove trajectories are resampled to match teleoperation speeds for co-training. Calibrating the glove's closed width to the teleoperated minimum ensured zero dropped objects during transport across 120 real-robot evaluation rollouts.

sections.heading: Real-robot experiments: The power of glove data and the head camera's edge
sections.summary: We evaluated glove label accuracy, co-training benefits with teleoperation data, and real-robot performance across different camera viewpoints. The head camera achieved a 20/25 success rate, resolving the dropped-object failures common with wrist cameras.
sections.details:
### Label Accuracy and Encoder Equivalency
When mounting the marker sphere directly on the robot and comparing vision-derived labels against ground-truth encoder readings, position error had a median of 6.5 mm (14.1 mm at the 90th percentile), and angular error was just 1.55°. Jaw width was estimated within a median of 3.5% of total stroke. A policy trained purely on these visual labels suffered only a 3% increase in validation loss compared to one trained on true encoder states, and achieved comparable real-world success (15/25 vs. 18/25, no statistically significant difference).

### Co-Training and Reducing Collection Costs
Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes via co-training boosted real-robot rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25. This matches the performance of a model trained on 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25). Log-linear interpolation suggests that the glove data equates to roughly 65 to 100 teleoperated episodes, substantially reducing the demand for expensive real robots and operator hours.

### Performance Discrepancies and Failure Modes by Viewpoint
Under identical training conditions, real-robot evaluations revealed distinct differences across camera perspectives:
- Head camera: 20/25 success
- Wrist fisheye camera (conventional UMI recipe): 15/25 success
- Fixed external camera: 12/25 success
- Head labels + wrist viewpoint: 14/25 success

The failure modes were especially revealing. Out of 21 failures with the wrist-camera policy, 12 were "drops during transport." Video analysis showed that after grasping and lifting the block, the basket (goal) completely vanished from the frame during rotation, causing the policy to release the object. In contrast, the head-camera policy dropped the object during transport only once (a slip during lift-off), with nearly all other failures occurring at the initial grasp. Keeping both the hand and the goal visible within a single frame plays a decisive role in robust task completion.

sections.heading: Limitations and future work: Glove-only transfer and bimanual scaling
sections.summary: We outline current limitations, including the collector's arm appearing in the frame (preventing glove-only training) and the follower arm's lag. Future work aims at extending to bimanual tasks and in-the-wild environments.
sections.details:
This study has several constraints and avenues for improvement.

First, because the collector's forearms and fingers appear in the head-camera footage, policies trained on glove data alone do not transfer well to the physical robot. Co-training with real teleoperation data remains necessary (validation loss degrades from 0.26 in co-training to 0.52 for glove-only).

Second, the viewpoint-mimicking arm has a 0.4-second response lag and can occasionally reach joint limits during fast, wide motions. In addition, this work evaluated a single workspace layout and one data collector; testing robustness across diverse environments and multiple human operators remains future work.

Nonetheless, the approach is highly scalable. By adding a second glove with distinct marker IDs, the system can scale to bimanual manipulation without adding any extra cameras or follower arms. Future work will explore bimanual tasks and validation in unconstrained (in-the-wild) environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Calibration details and follower arm control
sections.summary: This section covers camera framing procedures, geometric correction of tiles, the ridge regression model for the follower arm, and robustness evaluations of jaw width tracking.
sections.details:
### Alignment and Calibration
When putting on the head camera, the collector performs a one-time adjustment by looking at a fixation point 0.5 to 1 m away until their gaze matches the center of the preview screen. The follower arm tip uses the same GoPro mount, allowing tool-free camera swapping. The desk tile layout is re-optimized across multiple video frames, drastically reducing the 4-tile reprojection error from 3.4 px to 0.5 px RMS.

### Follower Arm Control Model
Using gripper positions derived from forward kinematics of the robot joints, a ridge regression model trained on roughly 100 demonstration episodes predicts the relative head displacement relative to the hand. This follows the human viewpoint with a median error of 46 mm / 5.4°, roughly half the error of a stationary camera (87 mm / 7.0°).

### Robustness of Jaw Width Estimation
Evaluations across 112 teleoperated episodes (around 24,000 frames) confirmed that jaw width estimation error remains remarkably stable at 2.8% to 4.8% of stroke across varying camera distances (0.4 to 0.8 m), viewing angles (40° to 87°), and workspace positions.

takeaways: Adopting a head camera paired with a follower arm instead of a wrist camera keeps both the hand and the workspace (goal) in the same frame, drastically preventing dropped-object failures during transport

Making the handheld device completely passive (printed fiducials only) and using a single head camera for both visual inputs and hand tracking fundamentally eliminates sensor synchronization and cabling headaches
Co-training inexpensive handheld device demonstrations with a modest amount of teleoperation data yields the value of two to three times as much real-robot data, doubling data collection throughput
limitations: Due to the visual domain gap caused by the collector's arms and hands appearing in the frame, training on glove data alone is currently insufficient, making co-training with teleoperation data mandatory
Reference marker tiles must remain visible on the tabletop, posing constraints for deployment in completely marker-free, arbitrary environments
The follower arm incurs a ~0.4 s tracking lag and may reach its kinematic limits during fast, wide-range motions
